sources.title: Action observation and acquired motor skills: an FMRI study with expert dancers
sources.authors: Calvo-Merino B, Glaser DE, Grèzes J, Passingham RE, Haggard P.

sources.title: Building a motor simulation de novo: observation of dance by dancers
sources.authors: Cross ES, Hamilton AF, Grafton ST.

sources.title: Sensitivity of the action observation network to physical and observational learning
sources.authors: Cross ES, Kraemer DJ, Hamilton AF, Kelley WM, Grafton ST.

sources.title: Motor simulation without motor expertise: enhanced corticospinal excitability in visually experienced dance spectators
sources.authors: Jola C, Abedian-Amiri A, Kuppuswamy A, Pollick FE, Grosbras MH.

findings.finding: Expert dancers show greater brain activation in premotor and parietal areas when watching movements from their own trained dance style compared to unfamiliar styles.
findings.quote: We found greater bilateral activations in premotor cortex and intraparietal sulcus, right superior parietal lobe and left posterior superior temporal sulcus when expert dancers viewed movements that they had been trained to perform compared to movements they had not.

findings.finding: Brain activity during action simulation is enhanced when learners have physical experience or practice with the observed movements.
findings.quote: Critically, inferior parietal lobule and ventral premotor activity was modulated as a function of dancers' ratings of their own ability to perform the observed movements and their motor experience.

findings.finding: Observational learning alone helps build action resonance processes in the brain even without immediate physical practice.
findings.quote: These imaging data demonstrate the emergence of action resonance processes in the human brain based on observational learning without physical practice and identify commonalities in the neural substrates for physical and observational learning.

findings.finding: Visual familiarity through frequent viewing of a specific dance style can enhance motor simulation and corticospinal excitability even without physical training.
findings.quote: We observed that frequent ballet spectators showed larger MEP amplitudes in the arm muscles when watching ballet compared to when they watched other performances.

principle: When people observe actions they already know or have seen before, their brain's mirror and motor areas simulate those movements more strongly.
for_the_teacher: Let learners watch dance sequences repeatedly to build visual familiarity and engage their motor simulation networks before they try to execute the movements.
